newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech cenbank sees 1996 c/a deficit at 7 pct/GDP.
newsitem.headline: Czech cenbank sees 1996 c/a deficit at 7 pct/GDP.

text.p: Czech National Bank Governor Josef Tosovsky said he expected the 1996 current account deficit to grow to seven percent of gross domestic product, up from four percent last year.

"In the first half this year, the deficit was $1.7 billion, and we expect it to be around $4 billion at the end of this year," Tosovsky said in an interview for Reuters Financial Television to be broadcast later. "It should be somewhere around seven percent of GDP."
The governor repeated the central bank's long-standing policy that an administrative devaluation of the Czech crown to help boost exports would not be necessary or desirable.

Some analysts and exporters have called for a devaluation of the still-strong crown to help narrow the trade gap, but others say the current account deficit can be financed at least in the short to medium term.

Tosovsky said the current account deficit -- caused by a merchandise trade gap which was well over 100 billion crowns in the first nine months of the year and surpassed the deficit for the whole of 1995 -- was not dangerous in the medium-term.
"We should not be afraid of the size of the deficit," Tosovsky said.
"If you would watch some other indicators such as gross debt... as a percent of GDP, or debt servicing... or the composition of reserves, you would see that we are far from any dangerous levels."
Tosovsky added that combined with continued prudence in fiscal policy "we can go through this situation, with a quite large deficit, at least in the medium-run."
When asked whether he would like to at least see the market rate of the crown ease somewhat to help exports even without an administrative devaluation, Tosovsky said:

"I certain would not like to see any devaluation. What I would like to see is a normal fluctuation of the exchange rate within the band which is seven and a half percent, up and down from central parity" of the mark/dollar basket to which it is fixed each day.
For months, the Czech crown has traded on the open market above parity with the central bank's mark/dollar basket.
On Friday the crown was at 26.888 to the dollar and 17.847 to the mark, or 2.45 percent above the basket, just under Thursday's level of 2.47 percent above parity.
